1:
All of them begin with the chain of transmission, and Barnes states it as a rule for the whole book: the word rendered revelation means an uncovering, and the Greek has no article, so this is a revelation and not the revelation, a title claiming no monopoly over Scripture. Whether the genitive names subject or author divides them briefly, until Barnes settles it on three grounds: God is said to have given it to him, it concerns things shortly to come to pass, and the book in fact discloses events rather than a person. Ellicott settles it by quoting Grotius — John is the writer but Jesus Christ is the author — and holds that only a living person could be the beginning of creation and its final rest. Wesley notes that no older prophecy carries this title, and reads the book as a manifesto where the Heir of all things declares all power is given him. Bede finds the reason for the veiling in the word signified: it was wrapped in mystical words lest it lie open to all and be lightly esteemed.

On how the book is to be read Clarke sets out four hypotheses and refuses to choose. It predicts the fall of Jerusalem and the Roman civil wars; or persecution under the heathen emperors and peace under the Christian ones; or the Roman pontiffs and the fall of their system; or the ruin of the Reformation — this last, he says, invented in retaliation, its boldest advocate having named a year now past while the Protestant churches stand. He adds no opinion of his own, quotes Graserus that the book is so obscure its explanation can scarcely be attempted without danger, and delivers a verdict on his own trade: the expositions of this book have done great disservice to religion, since almost every commentator has become a prophet, and disappointment has taught shallow readers to despise prophecy. Against that Ellicott holds the words of God to be of perpetual fulfilment, so that the principles are not exhausted by their first application; and Robertson makes the word for shortly a relative term, measured by God's clock and not ours, while granting that the early hope looked for a speedy return, and that the book must be read by the light of that hope and of the fires of persecution.

The blessing on the reader is taken two ways. Barnes prefers private reading, since the book was sent abroad to Christians and not merely to ministers, and adds a limit: the promise is not that the reader will understand, only that he is favoured to have it before him — though no author could call a man favoured for hearing words that meant nothing. Robertson takes the public reading instead, notes that the lector grew into an office, and remarks that Scripture reading in worship is still often badly done. Gill takes both, closet and family as well as church, and hears behind the change of number an allusion to the synagogue, where the law was not barely read but expounded. Victorinus makes the blessing practical: whoever takes pains over the reading may learn from it to do works; Bede has teacher and hearer blessed alike, a short labour followed by joys that do not end; and Henry builds a ladder of it: a privilege to have the oracles at all, a further one to hear them opened by those able to give the sense, and no blessing whatever until what is read is kept in memory, affection and practice. Ellicott finds in that word his strongest argument that the book belongs to no single age: what is to be kept must be capable of being kept now. Wesley says plainly that some have handled the book so badly that others are afraid to touch it, as though the beatitude ran backwards.
4:
Asia is neither the continent nor even the peninsula, and everyone who touches the word narrows it: Barnes runs through four senses and settles on the south-western district of which Ephesus was the capital, while Ellicott makes it the proconsular province, a strip of seaboard bounded by the Caycus, the Maeander, the Phrygian hills and the sea. Robertson adds that there were congregations at Troas, Colossae and Hierapolis besides, so the seven were chosen as the best points of communication with seven districts. Clarke agrees the seven were not all, and hears in the naming of the writer the manner of the older prophets, who set their own names at the head of what they had received. Why seven is answered the same way by nearly all of them, the number of completeness, though Ellicott takes it further, citing Philo on seven as unity developed in diversity, and arguing from it that the seals, trumpets and vials are not three successive periods but three aspects of one. The salutation itself breaks grammar, and the breach is deliberate: Robertson shows the writer using the correct construction in the very next line, so the nominative stands on purpose, to fix the eternity and unchangeableness of the Name.

What the seven spirits are is the chapter's sharpest division. Clarke says angels, and calls it most evident from the place, the number and the tradition, producing Raphael in Tobit as one of the seven who present the prayers of the saints, the Targum where God speaks to the seven angels standing before him, and the rabbinic picture of the throne as a Persian court with its seven ministers. Barnes canvasses the opinions one by one. That the phrase means God himself he rejects as tautology, and as impossible of one who sits on the throne rather than before it; that it means the manifold providence of God he calls far-fetched; the angel reading he attributes to Beza, Wetstein, Stuart and Clarke by name, and then decides against them for the Holy Spirit, chiefly because angels are nowhere called the Spirits of God and such language could not be proper of a creature. Ellicott reaches the same end faster, calling the angel view plainly untenable whatever weight of names supports it. Wesley argues it from the book's own habits: angels are never termed spirits here, and when all the angels stand up and worship, the seven spirits neither stand nor worship. Henry simply calls them the perfect Spirit in his diversity of gifts.

The three titles given to Christ are read as a plan of the whole. Ellicott makes them the Revealing Prophet, the Life-giving High Priest and the real Ruler of mankind, and presses the present tense of the last: the message comes not from one who will be but from one who is the true ruler of earthly powers, so that the habit of postponing his reign has obscured a present fact. He and Robertson both trace the firstborn to one psalm, where the promise runs that God will make him his firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth, and where the bow in the cloud is called the faithful witness. It is that same psalm Cyril is quoting when his passage breaks off, at the end of an argument that those who confess one God while denying the Father of Jesus Christ contradict their own prophets, who make the son say Thou art my Father. Robertson prefers the reading loosed to washed and marks the change of tense, since Christ loosed us once but loves us always. On the clause following, he and Clarke both take the better attested text to be a kingdom of priests rather than kings and priests, and Gill shows the phrase already turned that way by the Targums, and by the saying that all Israelites are sons of kings.
7:
Whether this coming is the fall of Jerusalem or the last advent splits them, and the two who state it plainly contradict each other outright. Clarke refers it to judgment on the enemies of the faith and probably to Jerusalem's destruction, since the pierced one was to be manifested to the incredulous Jews; he reads all the kindreds of the earth as all the tribes of the land, takes the verse as predicting the ruin of the Jewish state, and treats that as presumptive proof the book predates it. Gill rules the same reading out on a date. If the vision came in Domitian's last years, as the ancients report and the chronologers place it, it falls more than twenty years after Jerusalem fell and cannot describe it; nor can it be a spiritual coming to convert the Jews, since this one is personal, with clouds, and seen by every eye — and a conversion would not set all the kindreds of the earth lamenting, for the wicked would take little notice, the Jews would rejoice, and so would the converted Gentiles. Wesley refuses the choice: preparation for the coming began at Jerusalem's fall and goes on uninterrupted, which is why the book never says he will come but always that he cometh.

On the tribes the same fault line runs, though it closes further along. Wesley makes it a rule of the book that the word always means the Israelites, but grants that where a word for nations or peoples stands with it, as here, the rest of mankind is taken in too. Robertson goes at once to the spiritual Israel of Jews and Gentiles, and adds a bleak aside that no nation had then accepted Christ as Lord, nor has any since. On the mourning Ellicott draws the finest distinction in the chapter: the prophet described grief over one dead, but this is grief directed towards one who was dead and is alive, so that those who wail are turning towards him the sorrow they owed him at the tomb. Robertson notes that the verb for pierced occurs only here and in the Fourth Gospel, both times out of the same prophet and neither time from the Greek version, evidence to him that the writer used the Hebrew or a later translator. Barnes keeps the reference wide enough to cover any looking upon the pierced one, and notes that cloud is a fit emblem of majesty even among the heathen. Ellicott reports that Augustine found in the clouds the saints themselves, spread over the world like rain.

The last verse turns on two textual questions and yields a third disagreement about what it proves. Clarke and Ellicott agree that the beginning and the ending is not original — wanting, Clarke says, in almost every manuscript of importance, added as an explanatory note and crept in afterwards, and struck out by Griesbach; imported, Ellicott judges, from the book's closing chapter. Both he and Barnes give the rabbinic background, that from aleph to tav meant a thing entire: Adam transgressed the law and Abraham kept it from aleph to tav; Clarke adds that the two Greek letters together spell the verb to breathe, apt in a symbolic book for the one in whom we live and move. Then they part over what the title establishes. Gill calls it no small proof of the proper deity of Christ, and Ellicott calls the words a strong declaration of his divinity; Barnes agrees the language could belong to none but the true God and that the natural reference is to Jesus, yet will not use the verse as a proof-text, because the manuscripts now preferred read God where the received text reads Lord. Robertson resolves it the other way, noting that the speaker changes without announcement and that only here and in one later place is God himself brought in speaking.
9:
What the writer calls himself is noticed by all of them and pressed hardest by Henry, who observes that he values his relation to the church above his authority in it, and that Judas Iscariot may be an apostle but not a brother in the family of God. Robertson makes the same point grammatically, that the missing title is self-effacement rather than evidence, and that a single article binds tribulation, kingdom and patience into one picture; Ellicott adds that the patience is neither for Christ nor of Christ but drawn from him, and Wesley notes that the kingdom stands in the middle of the three. Wesley also traces the book's fortunes by that word, little esteemed by the Asiatic church after Constantine but treasured by the African churches and by the persecuted since, because it was given to a banished man and men in affliction relish it most. Who banished him nobody can agree: Clarke weighs Domitian, Claudius and Nero and thinks the last most probable, Wesley names Domitian and Nerva, and Henry observes that the writer does not say, since it becomes Christians to speak sparingly of such things.

Clarke then describes the island at length — barren, thirty miles round, a convent on a fortified hill, twenty women to every man, plentiful in partridges and rabbits and much infested by pirates — while Ellicott, citing Plumptre, remarks how little of Patmos gets into the book at all, so that at the farthest one may think of the blue water flushing like the plumage of a dove. Robertson keeps to ten miles long and half as wide. On the state John was in when the vision came, Barnes stands alone. The others take it of prophetic rapture: Wesley calls it a trance, insensible of outward things; Clarke says he received the Spirit of prophecy; Robertson makes it an ecstatic condition and not the normal spiritual state; Ellicott compares the abstraction of Socrates standing rapt for hours together. Barnes denies the ecstasy outright, reasoning that the command to write came only afterwards, and holds it was rather a high state of religious enjoyment such as any Christian may know.

The day is agreed on and its name is not. Gill argues from the abolition of the sabbath and from Justin Martyr, writing within fifty years, that the first day is meant; Ellicott rules out the futurist reading that would make it the day of judgment, notes the adjective was perhaps coined for the Lord's Supper and passed from the supper to the day, and reports that the Levant calls it so still. Robertson brings Deissmann's papyri to it, where the same word means imperial, and the first of each month was Emperor's Day, the day money payments fell due — a term already in use that Christians found easy to take over. Then the voice, which Clarke says came unexpectedly, the trumpet calculated to gather in every wandering thought as God prepared Moses to receive the law. Wesley has the apostle facing east, toward Asia and the churches he must write to, and observes that though every book of the New Testament was written by the will of God, none other was so expressly commanded to be written. Barnes, pressed by the barrenness of the place, sees no improbability in his finding materials there, since he was banished for preaching and not for writing, and Bunyan found them in Bedford jail. On the last verse Clarke and Ellicott report that the opening title is absent from the best copies and that Griesbach struck it out; Gill, granting the same omissions, keeps it as fitly retained to mark who is speaking. Robertson reads the order of the seven as a route, north from Ephesus and then east and south, with the whole book to be read and probably copied at each.
12:
Whether one lampstand stood there or seven is settled three different ways. Barnes says seven, standing apart and far enough from each other that the figure could stand among them, and denies the scene is the temple at all. Clarke says the opposite, that the reference is to the seven-branched stand at Jerusalem, and takes it as a hint that the temple was a type of the whole Christian church. Ellicott proposes a reconciliation: what was seen was very likely the old familiar branched candlestick, the one made known to everybody by the Arch of Titus, but with the seven churches fresh in mind the eye fell on the seven limbs and lights rather than the stand — especially, as Plumptre suggests, if the figure standing there hid part of the main stem. So the separateness of the churches and their union in the one light would both be shown at once. Robertson simply records that here the lampstands are separate; Wesley sets them in a circle and notices that the vision came gradually, the voice first and then what was behind him; and Henry keeps to what they are for, that the churches take their light from Christ and hold it out to others.

Barnes and Robertson both insist the phrase is like a son of man and not like the Son of man, since the Greek has no article and the received rendering would have the writer saying that Christ was like himself; Robertson puts it that he is like a son of man but is not a man, and Gill guards the same point from the other side, that what stood among the lampstands was not the human nature but the Son of God in a form like it. The robe and the girdle are read as priestly by everyone, Clarke calling it the high priest in his vestments and still discharging that office, Ellicott naming him the King-Priest and the Melchisedec of the epistle. Both Ellicott and Robertson note from Josephus that girding high was itself a mark of dignity, and Ellicott and Wesley agree on the meaning of the height: a man on a journey girds his loins, so a girdle at the breast is the repose of one who has finished his toil. On the white head the chapter divides. Clarke makes the whiteness pure radiance, the rays that the Romans called a nimbus. Barnes rejects that, since wool and snow are poor images for brightness, and Ellicott answers the objection that age would imply decay by pointing at the wigs of monarchs and judges.

The metal of the feet is a word found nowhere else, and each of them does something different with it. Robertson gives up and calls it in reality an unknown metal. Barnes takes it for a white brass and mentions the Vulgate's aurichalcum and the old electrum of four parts gold to one of silver. Clarke prefers the Corinthian brass that ran together, so the story went, when Mummius burnt the city and the statues of three metals melted into one; but he offers a plainer alternative, copper fused with calamine, and says he has often stood over those underground furnaces and seen the flame burst up through the earth, which always brought this verse back to him. Ellicott makes it a hybrid of Greek and Hebrew meaning whitened brass, and adds Plumptre's suggestion that such a trade word would be current in a city of metalworkers. Of the sword all agree it is the word, though Clarke points it at the rebellious Jews and the persecuting Romans while Ellicott makes it the only weapon permitted, so that whoever takes another to advance the kingdom perishes by the one he chose; Barnes finds the same figure in what Aristophanes said of the speech of Pericles, that it left its point fixed deep in the hearer.
17:
What made him fall is put in different registers. Clarke matches it to the prophets, the same effect on Ezekiel and Daniel. Wesley measures it against the man's own past: he had once leaned on that breast, and now, near seventy years later, a single glance strikes the aged apostle to the ground — from which he draws the rule that a great sinking of nature usually precedes a large communication of heavenly things. Barnes doubts that John recognised him at all, since sixty years had passed and the questions put later rather suggest he did not. Ellicott reads it as the felt consciousness of unworthiness, distinct from the pity that made Dante fall as a dead body falls; he sets beside it the pagan story of Semele consumed by the brightness she asked to see, and then turns the fear into evidence, since the man who said he was not worthy to have Christ under his roof was praised for the greatest faith in Israel. Wesley notices two more things: that the hand laid on him was the hand that held the stars, and that he is not addressed by name as the angels addressed Zechariah, but as by a master already known — his look terrifies, his speech strengthens.

The keys are agreed to mean authority and disputed in their reach. Clarke supplies the rabbinic form: four keys the Jerusalem Targum says God never trusts to angel or seraph, of rain, provision, the grave and the barren womb, and three another tract says are never given into an apostle's hand, of life, rain and resurrection. From this he concludes the second word here means the grave only, and neither hell nor the place of separate spirits. Ellicott corrects the order the English gives, since death comes first and then the unseen realm it ushers men into, and insists the second death is not in view. Robertson pictures that realm as a walled city, the keys given as we honour a man with the keys of a city. Wesley divides it, the body abiding in death and the soul in the unseen, both under one power, and then turns the verse into a question: Peter was given the keys of the kingdom, not these; how then does his supposed successor at Rome come by the keys of purgatory? Ellicott finds two wonders standing together, that the living One became dead and the dead One lives for ever; Gill holds the first title to its strictest sense, of one who has life in himself originally and underivatively and is the fountain of it to others.

The threefold commission is read as the plan of the book, and Wesley maps it to the chapters exactly, what was seen filling this first one, what is running to the end of the third, what shall be beginning at the fourth. Ellicott allows the middle term a wider sense, the eternal principles underlying history as well as the present state of the churches; Barnes warns that nothing can be argued from the phrase about how long the future runs, though he thinks it stretches far. On the stars the disagreement is ecclesiastical. Ellicott lists three readings — guardian angels, hard to square with words of reproof; the ideal embodiment of the congregation; and the chief pastor, which he calls the view generally adopted and thinks favoured by the imagery — and notes the title belonged to the synagogue president. Robertson prefers the plain sense of messenger, sent from the churches or to them. Barnes attacks the prelatical reading point by point: no such groupings of churches then existed, each city is given a church in the singular, and on that reading seven bishops replaced one at a stroke; then he closes the case by quoting Stillingfleet, a defender of prelacy, conceding the angel may stand for the order of presbyters.
